walkers:lore-tull-piece1: Rye-Home. The long rye. Rye in by noon, and all Ellesby drunk on it by dark. Not me. Walked the stubble with the lantern to study the light on the Greywold, for a picture I owe the corps hall. Doe at the edge. Alone. Walked straight at her, near enough to count her ribs, and she never ran. Never shifted a foot. Beast-craft, that's all. An old hind that's learned nobody hunts at Rye-Home. The eyes are wrong. Set forward, like a hunter's. Like mine. My lantern caught them as the light went, a red spark in each, side by side, and I called "Who's that at the edge?" before I'd thought. Took her for a man. Told nobody that. Feller's girl was out there before me, playing statues with her. Turns her back, counts, spins round. The doe plays it better than the child does. Feller came down off the clamps at dusk as ever, whistling that tune of his, and makes a hash of the middle every time. The doe turned to follow him the whole way down the lane. I'll have that hide. Not a mark on it. Six pennies raw at Hesk, twenty painted. So I paint her first, for the hall, while she stands for it. ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-tull-piece2: Leaf-fall. The hide-house. Primed the long hide, chalk-glue twice, laced it in the big frame and stood it in the hide-house door. Three panels, one treeline, like the boar hunt in the corps hall at Hesk. She came at noon and stood in the stubble. Painted her in the first panel. Looked up. She'd come on a pace, same pose to the hair. Painted her in the second. Looked up. Another pace. Third panel the same. Never once saw her walk. Sat out the light watching her with a dry brush, and she never stirred while I watched. Hand steady the whole sitting. Feller's gone. Went up to the clamps at dusk after some sound and never came down. Three days the men walked the Greywold calling him and found not a thread. Maud says three knocks at her door that evening, and nobody there. Feller drank. A man who drinks walks into a bog. Penn has written her into his Roll as the 'Walker', since she walks only when nobody looks. Every model I ever had walked only when nobody looked. She's an old hind gone strange. Penn wants blessed silver. All silver has over steel is the shine. Snares set along the edge of the rye. Steel wire. Steel will do. ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-tull-piece3: Late autumn. The lane. Down the lane at dusk with a brace of hares off the north line, and someone up on Feller's clamps whistling Feller's tune. A month since the search ended. Stood and heard it through. Whoever it was had the middle better than Feller ever did, and Feller whistled it down this lane every dusk I can remember. Some reaper's lad who thinks it a fine joke, whistling a lost man's tune at his widow's door. I'll find him and box his ears. Maud stood in her yard with her hand to her mouth. Didn't look at her. Penn has torches set down the lane every night now, door to chapel. Every one was out by morning. Not burnt down. Out, cold, with pitch left on every head. Not a breath of wind all night. The stubble never stirred. Sat in the hide-house door after, no lamp, to see for myself. Two red points at the edge, past the last torch. They went the long way round Feller's clamps, where the turf still glows. Kept well off. No deer likes fire. Snares along the edge still empty. She steps round them, every one. Painted the lane after, torches and all, with the lamp lit. Left it lit till dawn. The work wanted it. ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-tull-piece4: Deep winter. The snow by the clamps. Feller's clamps cold at last, snow on the turf. Sat up all night in the hide-house door, lamp out for once. She was there at first light, side-on by the near clamp, looking at me. Fifty paces. Steel arrow, my own fletching. Took her behind the shoulder, where a doe drops. She did not drop. She stood up. Not as a deer gets up; she was on her feet already. She stood up, and kept standing up, legs going long, back going long, the hide hanging off her like a coat off a peg, until she was a head taller than me. Then it came. Eleven in the quiver. Loosed eleven, and counted them. It came through the drifts. When I looked, it stood. When I nocked, it was nearer. The last took it at six paces, and it went down in the snow by the clamps. Laid out, a head longer than me. Thin and branching as a hazel stool. Dark wood under mismatched pelts. No antlers. No skull of any beast. The red was going out of its eyes, slow, like a coal in the wet. Put my hand where its eyes had been. Two knots like old pine, a red spark in each, warm through my glove. Tried my knife on one. It wouldn't come. The corps men at Hesk would give a winter's wage to see it. Writing this sat on the clamp, with my eyes on it. ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-tull-piece5: Deep winter, the day after. Skinned it where it lay, eyes on it the whole while. Had the coat off in one piece, and that's beast-craft, whatever Penn says. Doe-brown over the shoulders, more than one doe's worth, laid one over another like roof shingles. Under those, a fox's brush. A grey ruff, wolf by the guard hairs. Older scraps under that, thin as vellum. Finest coat I ever took off anything, and off nothing I could name. Went for Penn, to witness. Wanted it in his Roll, not just my word. Back inside the hour. Nothing on the snow. A long dent where it had lain, smooth all round. No drag. No tracks but mine going, and mine and Penn's coming. Wolves, I told him. Saw no wolf sign. Wolves all the same, like the doe left dead on Maud's step at first snow. The knots gone with it. Corps men say a thing's eyes only come away when it's truly ended. Corps men say a great many things. Walked the coat to Hesk at first light. Corps buyer turned it over a long while, gave 9 pennies, and wouldn't hang it in the hall. Painting it for the hall instead: me and the coat, and the thing in the snow behind. Penn has written ended, and thanks his nails. It was steel. And I have its coat, and a thing can't walk without its coat. Let it walk naked through the winter. ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-penn-piece1: The Roll. Rye-Home. Rye-Home, the feast day. The long rye is in. Tithes received at the chapel door, for the steward at Hesk: Of Feller, charcoal, three loads. Of Hobb, rye, nine sheaves, and a goose. Of Garrow, rye, six sheaves. Of Tull, furs, seven pelts, marten and fox. Two owed. Of the households with no rye, in pennies, five. Noted, as a curiosity. While the reapers cut the last of the long rye, a doe stood in what was left standing and did not run from them. They cut to within a few paces of her and she did not start at the scythes. When Garrow walked out to her she turned and went into the Greywold at a walk, not hurrying, and by dusk she was back at the edge. Her eyes take the lamplight red, as a cat's do. Tull asks that no man shoot her, for he wants the hide whole and means to paint her first. The Feller child plays at statues with her from the yard gate, and says the doe is winning. The reapers call it luck. I make no judgment and note it only. Harvest home. Thanks be. ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-penn-piece2: The Roll. Leaf-fall. Leaf-fall, the twelfth day. Tithe of charcoal from the Feller household remitted, the collier being lost. Jory Feller went up to his clamps at dusk on the ninth day, after a sound, and did not come down. There had been knocks at his door at dusk, with no one there: one knock on one evening, two on another, three on the evening he went. Hobb's boy kept the count, and the widow's agrees. We searched the Greywold three days, every man in Ellesby, and found no mark of him past the clamps. That night the doe stood again at the edge of the rye. She stands while she is looked at. Turn from her and she is nearer. No one has seen her walk. I write it here as the Walker, for it walks only when no one looks. At Hesk they are saying the Rot has come into the Greywold in a doe's shape. It has not. The Rot leaves nothing whole, and she is whole and sleek as a fatted calf. It is a devil. God keep Jory Feller, wherever he is. God keep Ellesby. ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-penn-piece3: The Roll. First snow. First snow, the sixth day. Since late autumn, one knock again at the Feller door, as it began before Jory went. At the first snow I set down rules for Ellesby, read them at every household and nailed them to the chapel door. The chapel's one silver candlestick is cut into nails, blessed, one for every door. The Feller door had the first. The Feller child drew two eyes above three strokes, to watch back, she said, and I have chalked it under every nail as a watching mark. I did not ask her what the strokes were. On the third day, at dusk, two knocks at Feller's. In the morning the door stood open and the hearth was cold. The widow had left the latch up for her husband. There were prints in the snow up to the sill, and on the sill, and none beyond. The resin was scuffed where it had stood. It came no further. The threshold was blessed at Rye-Home, and the nail was over it. Thanks be. To the rules I have added two: Bar the door at dusk, and lift the latch for no one. Let no one walk out alone after dusk. A petition for silver goes to the steward at Hesk. God keep Ellesby. ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-penn-piece4: The Roll. Deep winter. Deep winter, the eleventh day. Firewood to the chapel from every household. Thanks be. It is ended. I set it down in order. Tull came to my door this morning to have me witness. He says he put a steel arrow in the doe at fifty paces by the clamps, and she did not drop. She stood up, and went on standing up until she was a head taller than he, and came at him through the drifts. He loosed every arrow he had, and the last brought it down. What lay in the snow, he says, was no doe but a tall thing in furs, thin and branched, with dark wood beneath. He had skinned it before he came for me. I went with him. Where it had lain there was a long hollow in the snow, and no track to it or from it but Tull's own. Tull says wolves. I write wolves. I have seen the coat: doe-hide over doe-hide, a fox's brush, a grey ruff, and older scraps I could not name. There has been no third knock at Feller's. The blessed nails have held. It is ended. Thanks be. ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-quayle-piece1: How I came by them You've paid your gear, friend, so you may as well have it honest. At the tail of summer a treasure hunter came by the Tally Stone, mud to his knees and a sack on his back. He'd been through the ruin at Ellesby, where the rye's gone wild: the chapel, the hide-house, a cottage with a mark chalked on the door. Out of the sack came leaves of the reeve's roll, a trapper's daybook stiff with glue, and a child's drawings in charcoal. I gave him eleven gears and a dry blanket. He'd have taken less. They're from before the Holds, five centuries if a day. Before the gathering, before your tall returned sort, before any of us. And every page is about one thing: a doe that won't run. They called it the Walker, for it walks only when nobody's looking. I copy them fair and sell them by the sheet, every word as I found it, near enough. The drawings I won't sell. I pinned them back up in that cottage, where the child had them. Don't ask me why. Here's the lesson, free: Ellesby trusted chapel silver. Ellesby is nettles now. ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-quayle-piece2: Silver, and where to get it Ellesby knew it wanted silver. Their trouble was where they got it. The reeve cut the chapel candlestick into nails, soft stuff blessed thin, and look where that got them. Their nails were cheap chapel silver. Mine are proper. Two gears the nail. Honest prices. Or dig your own. Native silver comes up with galena and quartz, any prospector knows it. Smelt it to an ingot and a smith worth his anvil will draw you arrowheads. And if you've the gears, the luxuries man carries an ornate silver spear. Dear, but it's the real thing. Mind this, for I'd put my name to it: silver in it is not enough, the last one in must be silver. Why silver? Because it's honest metal, friend. Same as me. Don't trust a doe that stands and stares, nor a lone fox or wolf that does it. It wears what it likes. Its fur draws it to you, so burn anything it has brushed. In the old days an exile could buy her way back below with something of value. They say a pair of Walker's eyes would have done it. Nobody's offered me a pair yet. ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-quayle-piece3: A doe at the stone Here's a sheet no other trader can sell you, friend. None of them has the stall for it. A doe comes to the trees behind the Tally Stone at dusk. Same one each time. She stands side-on, head turned to the stall, and she never runs. Bang a pot, she stands. Holler, she stands. Look close and her eyes are on the front of her face, like yours and mine, with a red spark when the lamp catches. Walk out to her and she's gone before you arrive. I sell looks at her: one gear, from the stone. Don't look away, that's what you're paying for. Folk who look away swear she's a pace nearer when they look back. Folk who stare too long find they've been staring at trees. Nobody has seen her walk. Walled-village people walk two days for it, and not one has asked for their gear back. Where's she from? I'll be honest. Five centuries of nothing, then your tall returned sort come walking out of the woods, and now there's a doe at my stone. I say your tall returned sort brought it back with you. No offence meant. ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-quayle-piece4: I believe my own wares Folk ask whether I believe what I sell. Friend, I'll show you. At first frost I went down to the luxuries man with every gear I had: the stall money, the nail money, the sock under the floorboard. I came back with his ornate silver spear. Everything. He counted it twice and looked at me like I'd asked him to dance. It stands behind the counter now. You may look. You may not touch. There's a proper silver nail over the stall door, two more over the shutters, and the mark chalked under each, the way Ellesby had it. My fair copy of the rules is pinned inside the door. I read it every night before I put out the lamp. Last night at dusk, one knock on the stall door. Just the one. I didn't open. That's it watching. Let it watch. It'll see a woman with a silver spear and her nails up, and it can think on that. So when I tell you the last one in must be silver, I'm not selling you anything I haven't bought myself. Nails on the shelf, honest silver every one. Buy with confidence. ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-hide-piece1: 1. The Doe in the Rye The long rye at Rye-Home dusk, the sky copied off the hall picture at Hesk, the doe put in from life. No doe ever held still for her portrait before. This one stood the whole sitting and watched me work. Mind the eyes. I painted them as I saw them.
walkers:lore-hide-piece2: 2. Every Time I Looked Up Painted her three times on one hide, in one sitting, like the long boar hunt in the corps hall. Each time I looked up from the work she'd come on a pace through the stubble. Never once saw her walk. A good model, then. She holds still for you.
walkers:lore-hide-piece3: 3. Torches Out The lane, the night Penn had it lit end to end. Every torch out by morning, and not a breath of wind to do it. Put the red in where I saw it, at the edge, well off Feller's clamps. It kept off the glow, as any deer would. Painted by lamplight.
walkers:lore-hide-piece4: 4. The Finest Coat Finest coat I ever took off anything, and off nothing I could name. Nine pennies at Hesk. Let it walk naked through the winter. Over the dark shape in the drifts behind him, and not over the furs, a heavier hand than Tull's has daubed a fire in thick, bright orange.
walkers:lore-drawing-piece1: 1. Statues When I look she stops. When I look away she wins. Statues! You moved! I never see her move. Her eyes are on the front like ours. The Tall Doe is lonely so I play with her. Nobody else will.
walkers:lore-drawing-piece2: 2. Our Door The two are eyes so we watch back. The three is Mama and me and Papa. I still put Papa. She stood in our door. She did not come in. My drawing stopped her. Penn put it on every door. I didn't say he could.
walkers:lore-drawing-piece3: 3. Papa's Song She sings Papa's song. She does the middle right. Papa never did. She has lots of coats. One is a fox. No horns. She doesn't like my lantern. When I hold it up she stops.
walkers:lore-drawing-piece4: 4. Out of the Trees This is when she stood up out of the trees. She is taller than the low branches. Her doe is on the ground like a coat. She came out to play. Mama says don't draw her like that. I drew her.
walkers:lore-maud-piece1: Leaf-fall, the week Jory went Agathe, Jory's lost, not dead. Nobody's said dead, so don't say it to Mother. A knock at dusk one evening, only the one, and nobody there. Another evening two, and nobody. The evening he went it was three, and I opened to nothing but the rye, and after supper there was a sound up by the clamps and he took the lantern to see to it, and he never came down. They searched the Greywold three days. Not a print past the clamps. The night he went, the doe was back at the edge of the rye, the one that won't run. She stands too still, and her eyes sit too far forward and take the lamplight red. Tilde went to the shutter and said, "Something's moving out there." She wouldn't come away. I keep listening at the door for what he always said, as if I didn't know his step: "It's only me. Lift the latch, it's cold." Agathe, if this reaches you before the snow, ask the carters if anyone's seen a big fair man on the road, charcoal in the lines of his hands. Men do wander. I go to the clamps every evening and sing his tune, so he'll have something to walk home to. This goes to the Tally Stone for the carter. Your loving sister, Maud ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-maud-piece2: Late autumn, frost on the stubble Agathe, No word from you yet. The roads, I suppose. Tilde plays statues with the doe, like we did on the green. She looks and it stands like a post. She turns her back and it's nearer. She's never once caught it walking. Penn calls it the Walker now, for it walks only when nobody looks. Tilde says that's just statues. Today she was at the gate calling, "Mama, come out and see the doe." I went out with flour to my elbows, and there it stood at the end of the frosted stubble, nearer than ever, looking at the house. I looked back a long while, and then it turned and walked into the trees, not hurrying, and when I went to the place there was nothing. I told her what every mother in Ellesby says: "Mind your tongue at the edge. The Forest Saw That." I never knew why. Penn says it practises what it hears. I've called Jory from the clamps every evening since he went. If it's heard anybody, Agathe, it's heard me. Tull says steel will do. Penn says silver, and the smith at Hesk could draw arrowheads from silver, if Ellesby had any silver but the chapel candlestick. This goes to the Tally Stone for the carter. Your loving sister, Maud ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-maud-piece3: Late autumn, a month since Jory went Agathe, Don't show this to Mother. Last night I sat mending by the fire and heard my own feet cross the yard. The frozen ruts by the woodpile, the flagstone that rocks. Then our door, the long creak it gives on the hinge. Then the lid of the meal chest, the way it sticks, and that was out in the yard too, and the chest was at my elbow, shut. I had the needle in my hand. Tilde was asleep. Nobody had moved. Then, up by the clamps, whistling. His tune, the one he whistled coming down every evening. Wrong in the middle, the way he always got it wrong. Nobody else gets it wrong like that. He's out in the Greywold, and every evening I've sung it up there for him, and now he's whistling it back so I'll know. Tull says it's the doe. Tull says a great many things. I'll grant him this: every torch along the lane was out by morning, but whatever stands at the edge of an evening keeps off the clamps, where I've kept his last burn glowing under the turf. It goes the long way round. I'd like to think that's Jory's fire, keeping it off. I've left the latch up. He'll not have to stand out in the cold and ask. This goes to the Tally Stone for the carter. You've not answered, but the roads are bad. Your loving sister, Maud ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-maud-piece4: First snow Agathe, Two knocks at dusk, the night the snow came. Penn says two means it has learned you. He did our door himself: resin across the sill, the first nail cut from the chapel candlestick, and Tilde's drawing chalked under it. All but the bar. I left the latch up, for how is Jory to get in if it's barred? In the morning the door stood open and the hearth was cold. There were prints in the snow up to the sill, and on the sill, and none beyond. By the woodpile they were a doe's. At the door they weren't. They came right up under the silver nail, and the resin was trodden through where it stood. Tilde woke saying, "Mama, it was standing in the door." When I asked what, she said the Tall Doe. Penn says it can't cross a blessed threshold. Ours was blessed at Rye-Home. He says that's why it came no further, and never says why it came at all. Next dawn a doe lay dead by the step, not a mark on her, laid there neat as a gift. Tull turned her over and said wolf kill. Penn's rules are up everywhere, and one I know is for me: Bar the door at dusk, and lift the latch for no one. The candlestick is cut into nails, and Tilde's drawing is on every door in Ellesby. This goes to the Tally Stone for the carter. Your loving sister, Maud ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-maud-piece5: Midsummer Agathe, One knock at dusk. Only the one, and nobody there. Wat Hobb has notched the byre post every day since Tull shot it in the snow, and he says it's two seasons to the day. Penn said ended. He wrote it in his Roll, and we believed him because we wanted to. It didn't stand and stare this time. Last autumn it stood at the edge for days before it came a step nearer. This time it was halfway up the rye the first evening. It knew me already. By the week's end it was two knocks. And it came here, not to Tull's. Tull sat up all spring watching his own door with his bow across his knees. Tull killed it, and it came to me. The carter brought your letter at last, and I sat in the road to read it. You ask why I haven't written since leaf-fall, and are we well, and is it the roads. Agathe, I've left you one every week at the stone. Where have they gone? I've thought the wind, or boys, or the carter dropping them in a ditch. Is Mother well? You didn't say. This goes to the Tally Stone for the carter like the others, with a flat stone on top so the wind can't have it. If it was the wind. Your loving sister, Maud ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-maud-piece6: The eve of Rye-Home Agathe, Tilde said it at supper: "She does the middle right. Papa never did." And I sat with the spoon in my hand and knew. Jory never once got his tune right, not in nine summers. He went wrong in the middle and laughed. I'm the one who gets it right. I sang it at the clamps every evening I waited for him, and all that while it stood at the edge and listened. It learned it from me. All autumn I thought he was whistling back to me, and it was only ever me, coming out of the dark. The steward won't send silver. It's wanted for the Holds. So I gave Tull my wedding ring, and he drew one arrowhead from it. One, he says, is all a good shot needs. Three knocks at dusk tonight. They've all come to sit with us, for Penn says let no one walk out alone after dusk, and I think of every evening I sat at the clamps alone, singing to the trees. Wat has the boar spear and a torch. Tilde won't let go of her lantern. Tull sits by the door with his bow and the one arrow, and says he'll go close, so it sees him do it. It's whistling now, by the clamps. And still I listen for it to go wrong in the middle. I'm not going out. In the morning this goes to the Tally Stone for the carter. In the morning. Your loving sister, Maud ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-wat-piece1: COUNT. LATE AUTUMN I COUNT THEM. NOBODY ELSE DOES. LEAF-FALL AT FELLERS. I HEARD EVRY ONE FROM THE BYRE. ONE AT DUSK. NOBODY AT THE DOOR. TWO. ANOTHER DUSK. NOBODY. THREE. THAT NIGHT JORY WENT UP TO THE CLAMPS AFTER A SOUND. HE NEVER COME DOWN. ONE IS WATCHING. TWO HAS LEARNT YOU. THREE IS TONIGHT. I TOLD PENN. I TOLD TULL. NOBODY LISTENS TO A BYRE BOY. SALT ON THE BYRE SILL. A WHOLE CROCK. MAM WILL HAVE MY HIDE. I SEEN HER AT THE RYE EDGE. I SEEN HER BY THE CLAMPS. I SEEN HER PAST THE BYRE. ALL ONE EVENING. ONE AT EVERY EDGE. TULL SAYS ITS ONE OLD HIND. TULL DONT COUNT NOTHING. NOW ONE AGAIN AT FELLERS. ITS STARTED ON MAUD. COUNT THEM. ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-wat-piece2: COUNT. FIRST SNOW TWO AT FELLERS. DOOR WERE OPEN IN THE MORNING. NEXT IS THREE. PRINTS UP TO THE SILL. NONE PAST IT. TILDE SAYS IT STOOD IN THE DOOR. BAR THE DOOR. MAUD LEFT IT UP FOR JORY. I HEARD MAUDS FEET IN HER YARD. MAUD WERE INDOORS. PENN PUT HIS MARK ON EVRY DOOR. I KNOW WHAT IT SAYS. TWO EYES. THREE KNOCKS. THATS TONIGHT. I DONE THREE ON THE BYRE DOOR SO IT THINKS IT CAME ALREADY. ALL THE SILVER WENT ON DOORS. JORY WERE ON HIS OWN AT THE CLAMPS. MAUD SITS UP THERE ON HER OWN EVRY EVENING. IT WANTS YOU ON YOUR OWN. WHEN THREE COMES. TORCH ON IT. KEEP IT ON. IT GOES OUT QUICK SO HIT IT AGAIN. IT PUTS THE TORCHES OUT SO FIRE IS WHAT IT HATES. IT RUNS FOR WATER WHEN IT BURNS. KEEP IT OFF THE POND. WATCH IT TILL ITS CLOSE. THEN DONT TRUST IT. KEEP SOMEONE ON IT. IF IT FALLS BURN IT WHERE IT FALLS. DONT STOP FOR NOTHING. THE BOAR SPEAR IS IRON. I KEEP IT BY ME. NOBODY LISTENS. I WROTE IT DOWN ANYHOW. ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-wat-piece3: COUNT. AFTER RYE-HOME IT DIED ON MY SPEAR. NOT HIS ARROW. TULLS ARROW WENT IN. SILVER. IT NEVER STOPPED. TULL WENT OUT ON HIS OWN. CLOSE. SO IT SEES HIM DO IT. IT HAD HIM BEFORE HE COUD NOCK AGAIN. TILDE HELD IT FIRST. NOT HER LANTERN. HER EYES. I PUT THE BOAR SPEAR IN IT. IRON. IT WENT DOWN AND STOPPED. WE CARRIED TULL HOME. ALL OF US. NOBODY STAYD WITH IT. WE COME BACK WITH FIRE AND IT WERE GONE. NO DRAG. NO TRACKS. PENN WROTE ENDED. HE WROTE ENDED IN THE WINTER TOO. TULL SHOT THE DOE IN THE WINTER. SHE STOOD UP TALLER THAN HIM. HE SHOT IT DOWN AND TOOK ITS COAT AND WENT FOR PENN. NOBODY STAYD WITH IT THEN NEITHER. TULLS WINTER ONE COME BACK. NOT TO TULLS. TO FELLERS. TWO SEASONS TO THE DAY. I COUNTED. NOTCHES ON THE BYRE POST. IRON BIT IT. NOT ENOUGH. NEVER SHOOT THE DOE. COUNT TWO SEASONS. I STARTED NEW NOTCHES. NEXT TIME KEEP SOMEONE ON IT. BURN IT WHERE IT FALLS. ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-pennlate-piece1: The Roll. Midsummer. Midsummer, the eighteenth day. Tithe of hay to Hesk. On the eleventh day, at dusk, one knock at the Feller door, and no one there. I have turned back the leaves. Tull's arrow was the eleventh day of deep winter. It is two seasons to the day. Tull sat up all spring in his doorway with his bow across his knees, watching his own door. He said that if anything came back, it would come for the man who killed it. Nothing has come to Tull's. It came to Feller's. It did not stand in the rye to be looked at, as it did at Rye-Home. The knocks came faster. Last autumn a month went by between one knock and two. This time there were two at Feller's before the week was out. A letter came by the carter for the widow Feller, from her sister at Maidentown, asking why she has not written since leaf-fall. The widow says she has left a letter at the Tally Stone every week. The carter says he has had nothing from Ellesby since leaf-fall but the tithe. I record both. The steward's answer to our petition came by the same carter. No silver can be spared for Ellesby. All silver is wanted for the Holds. I wrote ended. ___NEWPAGE___
walkers:lore-pennlate-piece2: The Roll. Rye-Home, and the thaw. The eve of Rye-Home. No tithe taken. Three knocks at the Feller door at dusk. After dark it stood in the Feller yard, the tall thing in its coats, and the Feller child held it there with her lantern, and it did not move. Tull went out from among us alone, to within a few paces, so it would see him do it. His arrow was silver, drawn from the widow's ring. It struck. I saw it go in. Then it came the last paces faster than any eye could follow, and Tull was dead. Hobb's boy put the boar spear in it and it fell, and the red went out of its eyes. We carried Tull home, all of us. When we came back with fire, it was gone. The silver struck it. It is ended. Thanks be. The thaw. I have written ended twice. The first time it came back to Feller's door, not to Tull's, though it was Tull who killed it. Today it is two seasons since the spear. Tull told me once what the corps men at Hesk say: that a thing's eyes only come away when it is truly ended. We never looked for its eyes. We left it lying and carried him home. I did not write that down. We go down to the Holds today by the steward's order, every household. As we loaded the carts there was a doe at the edge of the rye. Tilde waved. ___NEWPAGE___

walkers:walkers-book-tale-title: The Doe That Would Not Run
walkers:walkers-book-tale-p1:
Mind your tongue at the edge, children, for the Forest Saw That. Never turn your back on a doe that won't run. Haven't you heard about Gil the swineherd's boy?

Well, Gil was a boy about your size, no cleverer than you lot and no stupider either, and every autumn he drove his father's pigs up under the beeches to fatten on the mast. It was easy work for a lazy boy. The pigs did the eating, and Gil did the lying about.

One day, lying about in the beech mast, he looked up, and there was a doe at the edge of the trees, side-on, watching him. Gil flapped his cap at her. She didn't run. He shouted. She didn't run. Any proper doe would have been over the hill by then, but this one only stood and looked at him, with her eyes set a little too far forward in her head, the way a hunter's are.
walkers:walkers-book-tale-p2:
Now, Gil thought that was a grand thing, a doe that wanted to play. So he played statues with her, the way you play it on the green. He'd turn his back and shut his eyes, then whip round quick, and there she'd be, still as a post, not a hair moving, and a pace nearer. Turn away, turn back, a pace nearer. He never once caught her walking. Not once, all that long afternoon.

When the light began to go, he turned his back on her to drive the pigs home. All the way down the lane he could hear the pigs grunting and the dry leaves going, and under that, something keeping step with him. When he stopped, it stopped. He didn't look round. He didn't want to lose the game.

When he got to the yard and looked back, there she was at the top of the lane, still as a gatepost, watching the house.
walkers:walkers-book-tale-p3:
Gil's mother said what her own mother used to say: never shoot a doe that won't run. But Gil's father only laughed. "A doe is a doe," said he, "and if she comes in my mast, she's a dinner."

That night there came a knock at the door. One knock, that's all. Gil's father opened it, and there was nobody there, only the lane and the dark. The next night, two knocks. Nobody there. On the third night, three knocks, and then, from down at the sty, somebody whistling. It was his father's own tune, the one he whistled driving the pigs, every note of it, just as he whistled it himself.

Well, Gil's father pulled on his boots. "Somebody's having a joke," said he, "with my own tune." And out he went to see who.

He never came back. They searched the beech woods and the lane and the far fields till the frost came, and they never found so much as a boot.
walkers:walkers-book-tale-p4:
Gil's mother cried a long while. Then she took her one silver penny, the one she had kept back against a hard winter, and had it blessed at the chapel, and she nailed it over the door. And the doe never came again.

Gil grew up and kept pigs of his own, and he never whistled, and he never turned his back on anything at the edge of the trees.

So they tell it at Hesk, and so I have set it down for the children of Ellesby. The knocks came, and the silver answered them. Trust in blessed silver, and God keep you.
walkers:walkers-book-accounts-p1:
Late summer.
9th. Bought of a treasure hunter, old papers out of the ruin. 11 gears and a blanket. Robbed him.
10th. Ink and paper, 8 gears.
12th. Nails off the ruin doors, 9, cleaned up bright. Cost me the walk.
15th. Rules copied fair, 10 sheets. Cut to fit.
walkers:walkers-book-accounts-p2:
Leaf-fall.
2nd. Sold 5 sheets, 5 gears. 1 nail, 2 gears.
6th. Doe at the stone at dusk. Didn't run. Sold looks, 3 gears.
9th. Looks, 11 gears. Walled-village party. Best day yet.
11th. Copied the same leaf twice and never knew it. The shifting, I expect.
walkers:walkers-book-accounts-p3:
1st, first frost. Paid the luxuries man for the ornate spear. Everything. Worth every gear.
2nd. Sold 3 nails, 6 gears. Rules, 2 sheets, 2 gears.
5th. One knock at the stall door at dusk. Let it watch. I'm ready for it.
6th. Lost a day again, or two. The stall leans in the mornings like a deck in a swell. I made it the second when I woke and the sixth by noon. Put down the sixth.
walkers:walkers-book-accounts-p4:
3rd. Two knocks last night. Boards do that in a frost.
1st. Dead doe by the step at dawn, not a mark on her. Hide, 3 gears.
3rd. Doe at the stone at dusk. Didn't look long.
2nd. Gone round the ruin for the last of the chapel nails. Back by dark.
walkers:walkers-parch-rules-p1:
RULES FOR ELLESBY
Set down by A. Penn, Reeve, at first snow, for every household.
1. A doe that does not run is no doe. Keep it in sight, and keep a man on it always. It walks only when unwatched.
2. Count the knocks. One: it watches. Two: it has learned you. Three: it comes that night.
3. Answer no whistle after dark, though it be a voice you know.
4. Carry fire past dusk. It puts out torches. Keep yours lit.
5. A silver nail, blessed, over every door, and the watching mark chalked beneath.
6. A line of resin across the sill at dusk.
7. It cannot cross a blessed threshold. Stay within.
8. Blessed silver wounds it as no steel can.
9. Should it fall, strip its coat and burn the coat first, then the rest.
Added, after the Feller door:
10. Bar the door at dusk, and lift the latch for no one.
11. Let no one walk out alone after dusk.
God keep Ellesby.
walkers:walkers-parch-assold-p1:
RULES OF ELLESBY
Copied fair from the old Roll by H. Quayle, at the Tally Stone. Honest prices.
1. A doe that won't run is no doe. Don't look away.
2. Count the knocks. One, it watches. Two, it knows you. Three, tonight.
3. Answer no whistle after dark.
4. A silver nail over the door and the mark chalked under. Proper silver, not chapel silver. Nails sold here.
5. Its fur draws it to you. Burn anything it has brushed.
6. It cannot cross a blessed threshold.
7. The last one in must be silver. Arrowheads to order.
8. Should it fall, strip its coat
walkers:walkers-parch-steward-p1:
NOTICE TO ELLESBY
From the Steward of Hesk, for the viscount, to the reeve and households of Ellesby.

The reeve's petition for silver is received and refused. No silver shall go on nails for doors. All silver is wanted for the Holds.

Of the beast complained of: the huntsmen corps are wanted elsewhere, and Ellesby keeps a trapper.

At the thaw every household shall go down to the Holds for the gathering, with what one cart will carry. None to stay above.

Given at Hesk, at midsummer.
walkers:walkers-parch-sale-p1:
BILL OF SALE
Received of the corps buyer at Hesk, for one coat, of many furs, dark, strange: 9 pennies.
Beast: not known.
Taken: deep winter, by Feller's clamps, Ellesby.
Sold as seen. Pelts sound. No slip, no moth.
C. Tull
walkers:walkers-parch-outside-title: If You Are Reading This From Outside
walkers:walkers-parch-outside-p1:
IF YOU ARE READING THIS FROM OUTSIDE
then it has seen you too. Come in. The bar's off. I leave it off for custom.
Before you lift the latch, look once at the treeline and count what's standing there. Then don't look away again until you're through the door.
I don't knock. Never have. Anything that knocks here isn't me, so don't open to it.
If you hear me calling from the stone, I'm not at the stone.
Nails on the shelf, two gears each. Leave them in the dish.
H. Q.
